questions.q: Which statement describes @zudojs/core best?
questions.explain: The core defines Module/BaseModule and ContextStorage, and createApplication builds a container, configuration, logger and runtime for you. It depends only on @zudojs/errors and @zudojs/constants.
options: An HTTP framework with routing and middleware
The kernel: the module contract, the execution context, and createApplication, which wires a complete application stack
A thin wrapper that re-exports @zudojs/runtime and @zudojs/lifecycle
The package the CLI uses to parse commands

questions.q: A project made by zudojs create: which package runs its modules, and where does its BaseModule come from?
questions.explain: The generated src/app.ts calls createRuntime, and the generated modules extend the core's BaseModule. The module contract is shared; the orchestrator differs.

questions.q: Why should you check the package of an import like createRuntime or Container?
questions.explain: The names overlap but the APIs do not: @zudojs/runtime's createRuntime(services, options) is not the core's, and the core's Container uses register(token, { useValue }) rather than registerValue.
options: Because one of them is deprecated
The core exports its own createRuntime, Container and LifecycleManager, which differ from the ones in @zudojs/runtime, @zudojs/container and @zudojs/lifecycle
Because TypeScript cannot tell them apart
It does not matter; they are aliases

questions.q: What is the difference between a module and a module definition (defineModule)?
questions.explain: Definitions are frozen descriptions. Because the application builds modules from factories, a stopped application can start again with new instances instead of reusing half-stopped ones.
options: A definition describes a module and holds a factory that builds it; the application builds instances when it starts, and can build fresh ones after a restart
A definition is the TypeScript type of a module
A definition is a module that has no hooks

questions.q: What is app.state right after await createApplication({ … }) returns?
questions.explain: createApplication initializes the application (and its participants) before returning. It starts nothing unless you pass autoStart: true; you call start().

questions.q: Definitions are listed as payments (needs orders), orders (needs inventory), inventory. In which order do the onInitialize hooks run?
questions.explain: The order comes from the dependencies, not from the list. Each module initializes after the modules it depends on; stopping reverses it.
options: Alphabetical: inventory, orders, payments, by coincidence

questions.q: The orders module declares only inventory. In its hook it calls context.getModuleContext("payments"), and payments is registered. What happens?
questions.explain: Only declared dependencies are reachable, so the declared graph is the real graph. hasModule("payments") answers false for the same reason.
options: It adds payments to the dependencies automatically

questions.q: Why is reaching an undeclared module forbidden rather than allowed "because it is there anyway"?
questions.explain: Declaring a dependency does two jobs: it orders startup and it documents the coupling. Access without declaring would defeat both.
options: The start order is computed from declared dependencies; an undeclared module might not be initialized yet, and the hidden coupling would break when modules change
Because modules run in separate processes

questions.q: What is the difference between context.getConfig("orders.maxItems") and context.requireConfig("orders.maxItems")?
questions.explain: Use requireConfig for settings the module cannot run without, so a missing value fails at startup instead of halfway through a request.
options: getConfig returns undefined when the setting is missing; requireConfig throws

questions.q: What problem does the execution context solve?
questions.explain: Built on AsyncLocalStorage, it follows the async work started inside run(), so a deep log() call knows its correlation id.
options: It makes async code run faster
Any function running on behalf of a request can read that request's ids (and values) without them being passed through every call
It serializes requests so they never overlap

questions.q: Inside storage.run(ctx, async () => { … }), which of these does not see ctx automatically?
questions.explain: Async propagation follows promises, timers and callbacks scheduled within the run. Your own data structures are not async resources, so a job stored and run later needs capture() and runSnapshot().
options: A setTimeout callback scheduled inside the run
A function you store in an array and call later from a worker loop outside the run

questions.q: What does storage.runDerived({ operation: "reserve-stock" }, fn) keep from the current context?
questions.explain: A derived context marks a stage of the same execution. It throws when no context is active, because there is nothing to derive from.
options: Nothing; it starts a new execution
The same executionId and correlationId, with the new operation and merged metadata

questions.q: When should code call storage.require() instead of storage.get()?
questions.explain: get() returns undefined outside a context, which is normal for start-up code. require() turns a missing context into an immediate error.
options: Where running outside an execution context is a bug, so it should fail loudly with ExecutionContextNotFoundError

questions.q: const b = a.set(USER, user) where a is a ContextValues. What is true?
questions.explain: Immutable updates mean code that received a never sees it change underneath it, which matters when collections are shared across async work.
options: b is a new collection with the value; a is unchanged
a now contains the user and b is undefined
It throws because values are frozen

questions.q: During a request that has a current user in its ContextValues, an event listener starts a new execution with storage.run(newContext, …). Does the listener see the request's user?
questions.explain: Carrying values into new work must be a decision: use runDerived, runWithValues or a snapshot.
options: Yes, values always flow into nested runs
No: a new execution starts without values, so one request's user or transaction cannot leak into unrelated work
Only if the listener is async

questions.q: Why is createContextKey<CurrentUser>("current-user") better than using the string "current-user" as a key?
questions.explain: Two libraries can both name a key "user"; two symbols are always different. And the type parameter makes the lookup type-safe.
options: The key carries the value's type, so values.require(KEY) returns a CurrentUser without a cast, and its inner symbol cannot collide with another key of the same name
Strings are not allowed as object keys

questions.q: A cart provider is registered as "scoped" in the application's container. What do two concurrent requests get, and what happens outside any request?
questions.explain: createApplication's container uses the current execution context as the scope. Failing outside any scope prevents one cart being shared by every customer.
options: One shared cart; outside a request, the same cart
One cart per request (the same one for every resolve inside it); outside a request, resolve throws DependencyResolutionError

questions.q: A module fails during start(). The application is failed. How do you try again?
questions.explain: start() from failed throws InvalidStateError. stop() cleans up, including participants, and a stopped application can start again.
options: Call stop() first (state becomes stopped), then start(), which builds a fresh runtime and fresh modules
It is impossible; create a new application

questions.q: In the published core, database fails to initialize, and orders (which depends on it) never initialized. Which onDestroy hooks run in the rollback?
questions.explain: That is how the published version behaves, so every onDestroy must be safe for a module that never initialized: check that a resource exists before releasing it.

questions.q: start() rejects with RuntimeInitializationError: Runtime module initializing failed. Where is the useful information?
questions.explain: The wrapper's message is generic. Log the cause chain, or you will read "initializing failed" without knowing that the database refused the connection.
options: In error.cause, which names the module and carries the original error message
Nowhere; the original error is discarded

questions.q: Why does a test pass signalTarget to createApplication?
questions.explain: With a fake target, the runtime registers its listeners there. The test calls them, checks the modules stopped, and the test runner keeps running.
options: So the test can deliver a fake SIGTERM and check graceful shutdown without the real process handling it
Because signals are disabled in tests
To send signals to other processes

questions.q: Why give each test application its own contextStorage: createContextStorage()?
questions.explain: getDefaultContextStorage() is shared on purpose, so all framework pieces agree in a normal app. Isolation is something you opt into.
options: The default storage does not work in tests
By default every application, logger and container share one process-wide storage; tests running applications in parallel could observe each other's contexts

questions.q: A handler logs logger.info("login", { email, password }) with the core's ConsoleLogger created with default options. What appears in the log?
questions.explain: Redaction is opt-in for the core logger. createLogRedactor() replaces values under sensitive names such as password, secret and token.
options: The password in plain text, unless the logger was created with redact: createLogRedactor()
Nothing; fields named password are dropped

questions.q: What is the default startup deadline of the core's runtime, and what is the risk?
questions.explain: startup.timeoutMs defaults to 0. Set a limit so a stuck start fails with RuntimeTimeoutError and your process manager can react.
options: 0, meaning none: a hook that hangs on an unreachable service hangs the whole start

questions.q: Write derive(context, overrides): return a new frozen object with every field of context, the fields of overrides on top, and metadata merged (overrides win). executionId must never change, even if overrides contains one.
questions.explain: Spreading copies; the original stays untouched. Writing executionId after the spread guarantees a stage never pretends to be a different execution.

questions.q: Write a tiny immutable Values class: new Values() is empty, set(key, value) returns a new Values, get(key) returns the value or undefined, size() counts entries. Keys are symbols.
questions.explain: Copying the map on every set is what makes sharing safe: anyone holding a keeps seeing exactly what was in it. The private field stops outside code from changing the map directly.

questions.q: The storage below only works for synchronous code. Add capture() (returns the current context) and runSnapshot(snapshot, fn) (runs fn with that context current, then restores the previous one), and use them so the queued job prints req-8.
questions.explain: The snapshot is taken while the request is current and restored around the job. The finally puts the previous context back even if the job throws.

questions.q: Write moduleContextFor(id, declared, registry) returning an object with hasModule(other) (true only when other is declared and registered) and getModule(other) (throws Error("Module \"ID\" did not declare \"OTHER\"") for an undeclared module, otherwise returns registry.get(other)).
questions.explain: The context is a narrow view: the registry holds everything, but a module only sees what it declared. Note how this message names the real mistake, unlike the published "requires missing module".
questions.expected:
true false 1.4.0
Module "orders" did not declare "mailer"

questions.q: Write redact(fields) that returns a copy of a flat object where every key containing password, secret or token (any capitalisation) has the value "[REDACTED]".
questions.explain: Redact by key name before a line is written, because once a password is in a log file it is copied to every system that reads logs. The core's createLogRedactor() does this with word-boundary matching, so a key like tokenizer is left alone.

questions.q: Write createApp(startModules) with state, start() and stop(). start() is allowed only from "initialized" or "stopped" (otherwise throw Error("cannot start from STATE")); it sets "running", or "failed" if startModules() throws (rethrow). stop() always sets "stopped".
questions.explain: This is the application's rule in miniature: a failed start must be cleaned up with stop() before another attempt, so nothing half-started is started twice.
questions.expected:
error: ECONNREFUSED
start -> failed
error: cannot start from failed
start -> failed
stop -> stopped
start -> running

questions.q: Write scoped(factory) returning resolve(scopeKey): the first call for a key creates an instance with factory(), later calls with the same key return the same instance, and a missing key (undefined) throws Error("no active scope").
questions.explain: A WeakMap keyed by the scope object (for the core, the execution context) lets each request's instance be garbage-collected when the request is gone.

questions.q: Write connectionModule(open) returning { initialize, destroy }. initialize() stores open()'s result. destroy() calls its close() once and prints closed; if nothing is open it prints nothing to close. It must be safe to call destroy() before initialize() and twice in a row.
questions.explain: Rollbacks call destroy hooks on modules that may never have initialized, and shutdown paths may run twice. Guarding on the resource itself makes both harmless.
questions.expected:
nothing to close
closed
nothing to close
